cases.interviewerQuestion: Bearer-token auth existed specifically because the extension can't share cookies with the main app's domain — what did that force you to rethink about session handling or security that you'd taken for granted in the cookie-based flow?
cases.tonyRaw: With cookies, the browser handles token transport and expiry for you and you mostly stop thinking about it. Moving to bearer tokens for the extension meant I had to be deliberate about where the token lived, how it got attached to every one of those 30-plus route handlers, and what happened when it expired mid-session instead of the browser just quietly re-sending a valid cookie. It also made me think harder about the attack surface — a token sitting in extension storage is a different risk profile than an httpOnly cookie, so I couldn't treat auth as a solved problem I inherited, I had to actively decide how it was scoped and handled on the extension side. That shift from "the browser handles this" to "I own this end to end" was the real mental adjustment.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What was actually happening in the undifferentiated store before the split—can you walk me through a specific stale-state or re-render bug that made it clear these three layers needed to be separated?
cases.tonyRaw: I don't have a specific bug report to point to with a name and stack trace, so I won't invent one, but the pattern was consistent: local UI state and server-persisted state were living in the same store as the realtime collaborative state, so a Liveblocks presence update or cursor change would trigger re-renders and cache reads that had nothing to do with it, and vice versa — a TanStack Query invalidation could clobber in-flight collaborative edits because they were sitting in the same undifferentiated bucket with no clear ownership boundary. The tell was that fixes in one area kept causing regressions in another that looked unrelated on the surface. Splitting it into three layers — Liveblocks for realtime collaborative state, TanStack Query for server-persisted state with its own cache invalidation rules, and a Context/reducer for local UI state — meant each layer only re-rendered and revalidated for the kind of change it actually owned, which is what killed that whole class of stale-state bugs rather than patching them one at a time.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Supporting two concurrent editor versions while integrating AI output into ProseMirror's typed node model sounds like it could double the surface area for bugs. What was the hardest part of keeping the state-management layer consistent across both versions?
cases.tonyRaw: The hardest part wasn't the AI integration itself, it was that ProseMirror's typed node model is strict about document shape, so whatever the AI generated had to be coerced into valid nodes before the editor would even accept it — and I had to do that twice, once for each editor version's schema, without letting the two implementations drift into different bugs. I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on the feature, and personally designed that state-management layer, so the discipline was writing the transformation logic in a way that was version-aware at the boundary but shared everywhere else. The alternative was maintaining two parallel pipelines, which would have doubled the bug surface exactly the way you're describing. Keeping one shared core with thin version-specific adapters was the tradeoff that made it maintainable.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You mention the computation was always server-side and the real work was the architectural port itself — what made porting the TypeORM logic into the new GraphQL API nontrivial, given the calculations weren't changing?
cases.tonyRaw: The nontrivial part wasn't the math, it was making sure the port preserved exact behavior while sitting inside a completely different data-fetching and resolver model. TypeORM logic tends to lean on lazy-loaded relations and query-time assumptions that don't map cleanly onto GraphQL's resolver graph, so I had to be careful that fields computed one way in the old path came out identical in the new one. Given these were trade metrics for high-volume trader accounts, a subtle discrepancy wouldn't throw an error, it would just quietly produce a wrong number, so I worked closely with stakeholders to validate calculation accuracy against the old implementation before trusting the new path.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You spent nine months iterating on the debounce delay and timing for the autosave hook — what made that tuning so hard to get right, and what signals told you a given delay was wrong?
cases.tonyRaw: The hard part wasn't picking a number, it was that the right delay depended on what the user was doing — fast typing needed a longer debounce so we weren't saving on every keystroke, but anything that felt like a deliberate pause needed to save quickly so people trusted it wasn't losing work. The signal that a delay was wrong was almost always user-perceived: either saves felt laggy and people started manually triggering saves out of anxiety, or we were firing so often that dirty-state tracking and network calls started stepping on each other. I ended up treating it less as one constant and more as something I kept re-tuning against actual usage patterns over those months, since synthetic testing never surfaced the same edge cases real editing sessions did.
